title: Dentures
blurb: Complete and partial dentures: the stages from primary impressions to fit, what you do at each visit, aftercare, common problems and relines.
question: A patient phones a week after her new upper denture was fitted. It has a sore spot, it lifts when she talks, and she wants to know whether she can file the rough edge herself and how she should clean it. What do you tell her?

teach.body: A denture is a removable prosthesis that replaces missing teeth and the gum and bone around them. A complete (full) denture replaces every tooth in an arch; a partial denture replaces some and is held by the natural teeth that are left. Most are acrylic (pink plastic), but partials are often made on a cobalt-chrome metal framework. An immediate denture is fitted on the day teeth are extracted. A dental technician makes each denture to the dentist's written prescription.

teach.caption: Clasps grip the natural teeth to help retention. Clinical dental technicians can also provide complete dentures directly to patients with no teeth.

1: prosthetics tray; 2: slow-speed handpiece with a trimming bur; 3: articulator holding models; 4: impression or model powder with a mixing bowl and measuring scoop; 5: shade guide; 6: an acrylic partial denture with wire clasps.

steps.sub: Bite (jaw relation) recorded; tooth shade and mould chosen

teach.caption: Partial dentures follow a similar path. A cobalt-chrome partial adds a visit to try in the metal framework.

items: Confirm the patient's identity, and that the case and lab work are theirs, before impressions or fitting.
Mix alginate to the manufacturer's water-to-powder ratio and load the tray evenly.
Ask the patient to keep still until the material sets: movement distorts the impression.
Rinse and disinfect impressions and returned work, then bag and label them.
Send every stage with the dentist's written prescription, and write down any changes agreed at try-in.
Give aftercare advice at the fit and book the review appointment.

teach.caption: Every problem goes back to the clinician. Patients should never trim, file, glue or bend a denture themselves.

teach.h: Cleaning and caring for a denture
teach.body: Clean the denture every day with a soft denture brush and soap or denture cleaner, gently, over a basin of water or a folded towel so it won't break if dropped. Regular cleaning prevents staining and plaque build-up. Never use hot or boiling water, which can warp acrylic, and don't use bleach on metal dentures. If advised, leave it out at night to rest the gums, stored in water or a cleaning solution so it doesn't dry out. Keep attending check-ups, even with no natural teeth.

After extractions the jawbone keeps shrinking (resorbing), fastest in the first months. The denture stays the same size, so it gradually loosens. A reline adds a new fitting surface to the existing denture, either chairside or in the lab using an impression taken inside the denture. Immediate dentures almost always need relining once healing has settled. A loose, rubbing denture can also cause sore areas, denture stomatitis or overgrowth of the gum.

teach.text: When a patient asks to fix a denture at home (glue it, file it, bend a clasp), the answer is always no. Book them in. Self-repair can make the fit worse, damage the soft tissues and leave a denture that can't be repaired properly.

items: Stages: primary impressions, secondary impressions, registration (bite), wax try-in, fit, review.
Check patient identity before impressions and before fitting.
Keep the patient still while the impression sets, and send every stage with a written prescription.
Clasps on partial dentures aid retention.
Problems or breakages: book a review or repair, never self-repair.
Clean daily and gently; no hot water; leave out at night if advised.

summary: You can now name the denture types, list the stages from primary impressions to review, explain your role at each visit, give clear aftercare advice, and recognise which patient complaints need a review or a repair.

A.q: A patient attends for the first stage of a new complete denture. Which material is most often used for the primary impressions in a stock tray?
options: Zinc phosphate
Alginate
Glass ionomer
Gutta-percha
A.why: Alginate in a stock tray is the usual choice for primary impressions; the lab uses the models to make special trays.

whyNot.0: Zinc phosphate is a luting cement, not an impression material.
whyNot.2: Glass ionomer is a filling and luting material.
whyNot.3: Gutta-percha is used to fill root canals.

A.q: What is the main purpose of the registration stage when making complete dentures?
options: To check the finished denture fits well
To take an accurate secondary impression
To record how the jaws bite together
To polish the acrylic before the fit
A.why: At registration the dentist uses wax bite blocks to record the jaw relationship (the bite), so the lab can set the teeth correctly.

whyNot.0: Checking the finished denture happens at the fit appointment.
whyNot.1: Secondary impressions are taken at the stage before registration.
whyNot.3: Polishing is done by the lab after the try-in, not at registration.

A.q: A patient's new denture has a sore spot a week after fitting. What is the best advice?
options: Smooth the area at home with an emery board
Leave the denture out until the gum has healed
Line the sore area with denture adhesive
Book an appointment so it can be adjusted
A.why: Sore spots are usually pressure points that the clinician can ease, so the patient should be seen.

whyNot.0: Patients must never trim a denture themselves; it can ruin the fit.
whyNot.1: Leaving it out indefinitely delays adapting to the denture without fixing the cause.
whyNot.2: Adhesive doesn't remove a pressure point and can mask the problem.

B.q: A completed denture has come back from the laboratory. Before it is fitted, what should the dental nurse confirm first?
options: The patient's details match the case
The articulator screw is tightened
The shade guide has been cleaned
The lab's polishing mop has been replaced
B.why: Checking the patient's identity against the lab case prevents the wrong denture being fitted.

whyNot.1: The articulator is lab equipment and doesn't affect who the denture belongs to.
whyNot.2: Shade guide cleaning is routine, not the first safety check before fitting.
whyNot.3: Polishing equipment has nothing to do with confirming the right patient.

B.q: While an alginate impression is setting for a partial denture, which factor would most reduce its accuracy?
options: The chair being lowered slightly
The patient moving before it sets
The operating light angled higher
The bracket table placed nearby
B.why: Any movement of the tray or patient before the material sets distorts the impression.

whyNot.0: Chair height doesn't affect the material once the tray is seated.
whyNot.2: Light angle affects visibility, not the set of the impression.
whyNot.3: Where the bracket table sits has no effect on accuracy.

B.q: What is the main purpose of the clasps on many partial dentures?
options: To protect the gums from food packing
To record the jaw relationship
To help the denture stay in place
To brighten the natural teeth
B.why: Clasps grip the natural teeth, aiding retention of the partial denture.

whyNot.0: Clasps don't cover or protect the gums.
whyNot.1: Jaw relations are recorded with bite blocks at the registration stage.
whyNot.3: Clasps have no effect on tooth colour.

C.q: A patient's complete denture has cracked across the middle. What is the best advice?
options: Glue the two halves together tonight
Soften the edges in boiling water
File the sharp edges and keep wearing it
Book an appointment for a repair
C.why: A fractured denture needs a professional repair; home repairs give a poor fit and can't be undone easily.

whyNot.0: Household glue is toxic, gives a poor fit and makes a proper repair harder.
whyNot.1: Boiling water warps acrylic and would ruin the denture.
whyNot.2: Filing and continuing to wear a cracked denture risks injury and a complete break.

C.q: A patient asks how to clean her new denture. Which advice is correct?
options: Soak it in very hot water to sterilise it
Store it dry overnight to stop staining
Scrub it with whitening toothpaste after meals
Brush it daily and gently with a soft brush
C.why: Daily gentle brushing with a soft brush and soap or denture cleaner removes plaque and prevents staining without damaging the acrylic.

whyNot.0: Hot water can warp acrylic and spoil the fit.
whyNot.1: Dentures stored dry can dry out and distort; they should be kept moist.
whyNot.2: Abrasive toothpastes scratch acrylic, which then collects stain and plaque.

C.q: Why are dentures that were fitted immediately after extractions usually relined a few months later?
options: The bone shrinks as the sockets heal
The acrylic shrinks as it ages
The clasps loosen with daily cleaning
The teeth wear down from chewing
C.why: The bone resorbs as the sockets heal, so the denture loosens and needs a new fitting surface.

whyNot.1: Acrylic is dimensionally stable in normal use; the change is in the patient's jaw.
whyNot.2: Immediate dentures may have no clasps, and cleaning doesn't explain a general loss of fit.
whyNot.3: Tooth wear takes years and isn't why immediate dentures are relined.

reteach.title: Making a denture is like a made-to-measure suit
reteach.question: A tailor measures you, makes a rough version, has you try it on, then finishes it. How does each denture visit match that?

blocks.body: The primary impression is the quick first measurement. The secondary impression, in a tray made just for that patient, is the accurate measurement. Registration is checking how you stand and move: how the jaws bite. The wax try-in is the fitting room, where anything can still change. The fit is collection day, and the review is coming back to have it taken in where it pinches.

blocks.text: The wax try-in is the last chance to change the teeth. Once the lab processes the denture in acrylic, the tooth positions are fixed, so write down every change agreed with the patient.

explain.body: Complete dentures replace every tooth in an arch and rely on suction, muscles and fit. Partial dentures replace some teeth and use clasps on the remaining teeth. Partials can be acrylic or have a cobalt-chrome metal framework.

explain.caption: Several missing lower teeth with natural teeth remaining: a partial denture case.

test.q: What mainly keeps a complete upper denture in place?
options: Clasps on the natural teeth
Cement applied by the dentist
Suction, muscle control and fit
Screws into the palate
test.why: With no teeth to clasp, a complete denture relies on a close fit, suction and the patient's muscle control.

whyNot.0: A complete denture has no natural teeth to clasp.
whyNot.1: Dentures are removable, so they are never cemented.
whyNot.3: Screws into bone describe implants, not a conventional denture.

explain.body: Primary impressions, secondary impressions, registration, wax try-in, fit and review. The lab works between each visit, always to a written prescription.

test.q: At the wax try-in, the patient asks for the front teeth to look less even. What should happen next?
options: Record the changes for the laboratory
Tell the patient it is too late to change
Fit the denture and adjust it at review
Take new primary impressions
test.why: The try-in exists so changes can be agreed and recorded on the prescription before the denture is finished.

whyNot.1: Changes to tooth position are still possible at try-in.
whyNot.2: The denture can't be fitted until it has been processed in acrylic.
whyNot.3: New impressions aren't needed to change tooth arrangement.

explain.body: Sore spots, looseness, lifting when speaking, clicking, uneven bite, food packing under a partial and fractures all need the clinician. Pain when putting the denture in can mean an over-extended flange.

test.q: A patient says their new lower denture hurts as they put it in, and the edge digs into the gum. What is the likely cause?
options: The shade is too dark
The flange is over-extended
The clasps are too loose
The teeth are too small
test.why: An over-extended flange presses into the soft tissue, causing pain on insertion; the clinician can trim it back.

whyNot.2: Loose clasps cause looseness, not pain from the edge.
whyNot.3: Tooth size affects appearance and bite, not the flange edge.

explain.body: Clean daily and gently with a soft brush over water or a towel. No hot water, no bleach on metal, no abrasive toothpaste. Leave out at night if advised to rest the tissues, and keep it moist.

test.q: Why might a dentist advise a patient to remove their denture at night?
options: To rest the gums underneath
To harden the acrylic
To tighten the bite
To whiten the teeth
test.why: Removing the denture overnight lets the supporting tissues rest and reduces the risk of denture stomatitis.

whyNot.2: The bite isn't changed by leaving the denture out.
whyNot.3: Leaving it out doesn't whiten the teeth; cleaning prevents staining.
